[L61] The Frameworks, and the One Thing Underneath Them
[L62] I write with four master lenses. They are not four competing systems; they are four views
[L63] of the same underlying thing, a person under rising pressure forced to change. Here is what
[L64] each one is for, so I always know which tool I am holding.

[L66]   • Blake Snyder (Save the Cat), the spine. The fifteen beats in order, and the board
[L67]      that expands them into scenes. This is the skeleton the whole book hangs on. For a
[L68]      novel I use Jessica Brody's adaptation, which places the beats by percentage of the
[L69]      manuscript instead of by script page.
[L70]   • Robert McKee (Story), the depth. The controlling idea, the gap between
[L71]      expectation and result, the forces of antagonism, and the value scale. McKee tells
[L72]      me what is really at stake underneath the plot, and reminds me that a story is only
[L73]      as strong as its forces of antagonism, strength, not villainy.
[L74]   • K.M. Weiland (Creating Character Arcs, Structuring My Novel), the arc. The Lie

[L76]      versus the Need (the Truth), and the three arc types: Positive Change, Flat, and
[L77]      Negative. Weiland tells me how the inside of a character changes in step with the
[L78]      outside, beat by beat.

[L112] Part One: The Core (Snowflake Steps 1 and 2)
[L113] The Snowflake grows a story from one sentence outward. So does this bible. We start at the
[L114] smallest, truest description and expand. Get these first pieces right and everything after
[L115] them has a home.

[L117] The One Sentence (the Logline)
[L118] What it is. The logline is one sentence, under about twenty-five words, that captures the
[L119] whole book. Ingermanson calls it a marketing tool I memorize so I can say it without
[L120] thinking. Snyder says a strong one has four things: irony (something ironic and
[L121] emotionally involving, the hook), a compelling mental picture (I can see the whole story,
[L122] and guess how long it runs), the audience and the cost (for a novel, the audience and the
[L123] tone), and a killer title. It is also a diagnostic, not decoration: if I cannot state the irony in
[L124] one sentence, the problem may not be the logline, it may be that the story is not clear yet.
[L125] Build it first to prove the story has a spine.

[L127] Why it works, and the trap. Under the checklist is one idea: a logline is the whole book
[L128] squeezed until only its central irony is left. That is why irony is first and load-bearing.
[L129] Irony is the gap between what a character is doing and what is really going on, and that
[L130] gap is the difference between a situation and a story. “Two neighbors feud” is a situation;
[L131] anyone can picture it and nothing pulls. “Two neighbors feud, never seeing that the quiet
[L132] woman across the street started it and is winning” is a story, because now there is a gap
[L133] the reader wants closed. The trap is treating the logline as a blurb, a line to sell the book.
[L134] It is really a test. If the one sentence has no irony, the problem is almost never the
[L135] sentence. It is that the story does not have its gap yet, and the logline only made that
[L136] visible early, while it is still cheap to fix.

[L138] My board's template. The Save the Cat board on my wall gives a fill-in version, and I
[L139] reserve the right to modify it, which I should: “On the verge of [stasis equals death], a
[L140] [flawed protagonist] breaks into two, but when [the midpoint happens], he or she must
[L141] learn [the theme] before [all is lost].”

[L169] The One Paragraph (the Three-Act Spine)
[L170] What it is. Ingermanson expands the sentence into a five-sentence paragraph: one
[L171] sentence for the setup, then three disasters, then the ending. Disaster one ends Act One
[L172] and forces my lead to commit to the story. Disaster two ends the first half of Act Two and
[L173] flips the character from a false Moral Premise to a true one, so they commit to a new way
[L174] of thinking for the second half. Disaster three ends the second half of Act Two and forces
[L175] the commitment to end the story. His refinement: the second and third disasters should
[L176] be caused by the protagonist's own efforts to fix things. The purpose is a sound three-act
[L177] shape with three real disasters and a clear Moral Premise.

[L179] Why disasters, and not just events. The word disaster is doing precise work here, so
[L180] slow down on it. A disaster is not merely a bad thing that happens. It is a turn that forces
[L181] a choice the character cannot walk back, so the story cannot return to how it was. That is
[L182] why three disasters, and not ten events, carry the whole paragraph: each one locks a
[L183] door behind the character and pushes them into the next stretch. And Ingermanson's
[L184] refinement, that disasters two and three come from the protagonist's own attempts to fix
[L185] things, is what separates a story from a run of bad luck. When the roof caves in on a
[L186] character, we sympathize. When the character pulls the roof down himself while trying
[L187] to fix the ceiling, we lean in, because now the trouble is his and the comeuppance is
[L188] earned. For these men, that means the war has to spiral out of their own escalation,
[L189] never out of accident.

[L191] Cross-framework note. Disaster one is Snyder's Break into Two and Weiland's First Plot
[L192] Point. Disaster two sits near the Midpoint, the Moment of Truth where the character

[L202] A Disaster Is Not a Win, and Where the Ledger Sits
[L203] A disaster is a reversal, never a win. This nuance is worth pulling out on its own,
[L204] because getting it wrong tangles the back half of the book. A disaster, in this structure, is
[L205] a reversal. The definition: a turn where the character's plan fails and the ground shifts
[L206] under him, forcing a choice he cannot walk back. All three disasters are reversals, never
[L207] victories. Even when a disaster hands the character something useful, its felt content is
[L208] loss, because loss under pressure is what drives him into the next act. A beat that leaves
[L209] the character better off and in control is not a disaster, however eventful it looks.

[L211] Finding is not winning. That leads to a distinction this book lives on, so name it and
[L212] never blur it. A discovery is the moment a hidden truth lands on the character; it is
[L213] information, and here it is a gut-punch. A win is a moment the character acts and comes
[L214] out ahead; it is leverage played. Different beats, different places on the spine. For I
[L215] Declare War, the men discovering Francine's ledger is the reveal, and the reveal belongs
[L216] at disaster three, All Is Lost, because reading that book guts them: it was the old lady the
[L217] whole time, the war was a farce, they made fools of themselves. That devastation is the
[L218] reversal. The same book also handing them a card to play does not turn the discovery
[L219] into a win; it makes the discovery the hook that drags them into Act Three carrying new
[L220] leverage.

[L222] So where each piece sits. The win comes later, in the finale, when they pick the ledger
[L223] up and wield it, their one real card against a woman they could never out-think, and she
[L224] takes the war back warmly anyway. So the order holds: discovery at disaster three, the
[L225] gut-punch; wielding it in the finale, the one real win; her grace, the larger victory that
[L226] keeps her whole. That also clarifies disasters one and two, which should both be the
[L227] men's plans failing, reversals aimed squarely at them. One is the wrong that lights the
[L228] war and commits them. Two is the spiral and the public humiliation that force them to
[L229] stop and admit they have been played, without yet knowing by whom. Three turns, each
[L230] a loss for the men, each forcing a harder choice, and the hardest, the discovery, saved for
last.

[L259] The Moral Premise
[L260] What it is. The Moral Premise, from Stanley Williams, is my story's thematic truth
[L261] written as a cause-and-effect equation with four parts: a virtue, a vice, and their
[L262] consequences. The formal shape is: [Vice] leads to defeat, but [Virtue] leads to success.
[L263] Williams's claim is that every external obstacle in the story is really rooted in one
[L264] internal, moral obstacle, and the Moral Premise states that truth in a single line. Once I
[L265] know it, I structure the whole book around it, so every character and scene shadows the
[L266] same premise. This is the same thing McKee calls the controlling idea (Value plus Cause)
[L267] and Weiland calls the Lie versus the Truth. It is the spine under all my frameworks.

[L269] Why an equation, and not just a theme. Most writers carry a theme as a single word,
[L270] respect, or family, or loneliness, and a single word cannot structure a book, because it
[L271] names a topic without saying what the book claims about it. The Moral Premise forces
[L272] the claim into cause and effect: this vice leads to that defeat, this virtue leads to that
[L273] success. Once it is an equation, it becomes a test every scene has to pass. A scene either
[L274] shows the vice costing someone, or the virtue paying off, or a character crossing from
[L275] one to the other, and a scene that does none of those is probably not earning its place.
[L276] That is the difference between a theme I admire and a premise I can build on. The topic
[L277] is respect; the premise is what my book insists is true about respect.

[L285] (they believe the vice gets them what they want). At disaster two, near the midpoint, they
[L286] flip to the true half. The back half of the book proves the true premise through
[L287] consequence.

[L314] Ingermanson says every character is the lead of their own personal story. So each of my
[L315] three is a full person with their own values, their own arc, and their own forces pushing
[L316] against them. We build each one through all four lenses at once, because that is where they
[L317] come alive. For each character I get the teaching, an example of what could fill each slot,
[L318] and the blank handed back to me.

[L320] A note on the deepest tool here. Ingermanson finds a character's Values by having me
[L321] finish this sentence for them as many ways as I can: “Nothing is more important than
[L322] ______.” Most people land on two or three, and a strong story comes from putting those
[L323] two or three in conflict. His own example is Vito Corleone, who says instantly “Nothing is
[L324] more important than respect,” then adds “nothing is more important than family,” and
[L325] the whole Godfather saga lives in the collision of those two. Respect is also my book's
[L326] controlling value, which is a good omen. Use this sentence on all three of my leads. It is
[L327] the fastest way to the center of a person.

[L347] Ingermanson Sheet: Values, Ambition, Goal
[L348] What it is. The sheet is Role, Name, Goal (the concrete thing he wants in this story),
[L349] Ambition (the abstract thing underneath it), Values (his “nothing is more important
[L350] than” answers, in conflict), Conflict (what blocks the goal), and Epiphany (what he
[L351] learns). The Goal is concrete and reachable; the Ambition is the abstract hunger under it;
[L352] the Values are the core truths that make him act.

[L354] Why goal and ambition are two different things. The one distinction that makes this
[L355] sheet worth filling is the split between the goal and the ambition, because they are not
[L356] the same want wearing two hats. The goal is concrete and reachable, the thing he could
[L357] physically achieve and check off: win the war, prove Anthony did it. The ambition is the
[L358] abstract hunger underneath, the thing the goal is secretly standing in for: to be taken
[L359] seriously, to matter. A character chasing only a goal is thin, a man doing tasks. A
[L360] character whose goal is quietly carrying an ambition is deep, because every move
[L361] toward the small concrete thing is really a reach for the large unspeakable one. For
[L362] comedy this is where the gold is: Kevin fighting to win a dog-poop war, the goal, while
[L363] what he actually wants is to not be the fool, the ambition, is funny and sad at the same
[L364] time, and the gap between the two is where his truest and most ridiculous choices come
from.

[L388] Weiland Arc: Lie, Ghost, Want, Need
[L389] What it is. Kevin is almost certainly a Positive Change Arc: he starts believing a Lie, and
[L390] the story teaches him the Truth. The Lie is a false belief about himself or the world that
[L391] feels like protection. The Ghost is the wound in his past that planted the Lie. The Want is
[L392] his external goal, which is driven by the Lie. The Need is the Truth, the thing that actually
[L393] heals him, usually the opposite of what he is chasing.

[L395] How the four pieces interlock, and the three arc types. These four are not a list, they
[L396] are a chain, and seeing the chain is the point. The Ghost is a wound in the past. The
[L397] wound plants the Lie, a false belief that felt like protection at the time. The Lie drives the
[L398] Want, the external thing he chases because he believes it will keep him safe. And the
[L399] Need is the Truth that would actually heal him, almost always the opposite of the Want.
[L400] The Ghost is what lets us forgive the Lie: a man is not foolish for believing something that
[L401] once kept him safe, which is exactly what keeps Kevin sympathetic instead of merely
[L402] annoying. As for the shape of the change, Weiland names three arcs. A Positive Change
[L403] arc, where the character learns the Truth and is healed, almost certainly Kevin. A Flat
[L404] arc, where the character already holds the Truth and uses it to change everyone around
[L405] him, which is Francine on respect. And a Negative arc, where the character falls. Choose
[L406] the arc by deciding where I want him to end, and then the Lie is simply whatever he has
[L407] to stop believing to get there.

[L427] McKee: His Value and the Forces Against Him
[L428] What it is. Every main character needs forces of antagonism strong enough to make
[L429] them walk their value's full scale, and those forces work at three levels: inner (his own
[L430] psychology), personal (the people close to him), and extra-personal (the wider world and
[L431] situation). The forces do not have to be evil; they have to be strong, closing his easy exits
[L432] so he can only get what he wants by escalating.

[L434] Why the forces must close every exit, and the value scale. Two ideas make this more
[L435] than a list of opponents. First, the forces have to close every easy exit, and that is not
[L436] cruelty for its own sake, it is the only way to see who a character really is. A person with
[L437] an open door never has to choose; give him an escape and he takes it and the story stalls.
[L438] Shut every door and he must act, and the thing he does under maximum pressure, with
[L439] no good options left, is the truest thing the book can show about him. Second, the value
[L440] runs on a scale, and the story drives it downward. Respect is not simply present or
[L441] absent. It runs from respect, to disrespect, to humiliation, and at the very bottom to its
[L442] worst form, contempt wearing a polite face, honor said to a man's face and scorn behind
[L443] his back. The three levels, inner, personal, and larger than personal, are just the three
[L444] directions the pressure comes from, and all three have to press at once, because one
[L445] open direction becomes the exit that lets the air out. For a character-driven comedy the
[L446] inner level matters most: the strongest force against Kevin is Kevin.

[L704] frameworks, because they are all the same turns. Take my target word count and the
[L705] percentages give me rough landmarks: for a 90,000-word novel, the Catalyst lands near
[L706] word 9,000, the Midpoint near 45,000, All Is Lost near 67,000. The percentages are guides,
[L707] not rules. The beat sheet tells me when a turn happens; what happens is mine.

[L709] How to use this part when stuck: find the one beat I am on, read only it, look at the
[L710] example, and write one sentence of my version. That is a full unit of progress.

[L713] Also known as: Crossing tools call this the Ordinary World and the hero's current state, the

[L715] Final Image will later mirror to prove change.
[L716] What this beat really does. Every story opens on a world that is about to be disturbed,
[L717] and the opening image is the writer's one free photograph of that world before anything
[L718] changes. Its real job is not to start the action; it is to set the baseline the ending will
[L719] measure against. Whatever is broken, missing, or asleep in the hero at the start is what
[L720] the final image will later show healed, found, or awake, so the two pictures rhyme and
[L721] the reader feels the distance traveled without being told. The common misunderstanding
[L722] is to treat it as a hook, a loud cold open. It is nearly the opposite: a quiet, honest snapshot
[L723] chosen so that when you mirror it at the very end, the change lands. If nothing in the
[L724] opening can be turned over later, it is not yet doing its job.

[L726] What it is. A snapshot of the street in uneasy peace: Kevin in his driveway, polishing the
[L727] car he doesn't quite trust, side-eyeing Anthony's house; Anthony watching him with dry
[L728] amusement; and across the street, barely noticed by anyone including the reader,
[L729] Francine on her porch beside her garden. The image should quietly contain all three and
[L730] center the men, so the reader's eye slides past Francine exactly as the neighborhood
does.

[L734] flawed, divided world and quietly plant the thing the Final Image will later turn over.

[L736] when it is only scene-setting, a pretty establishing shot that sets up nothing that will
[L737] change, so the Final Image has no before to mirror. For this book it also fails if you open

[L889] the stretch where the hero weighs whether to step through the door. Its job is to make

[L891] weight and tells us nothing about the chooser. It is also where the reader's own doubt

[L893] the debate is usually short and funny, the hero performing reasonableness while
[L894] everyone can see where he is headed. The misunderstanding is to skip it, so the leap into
[L895] the story is free and the character shallow, or to let it run so long the story stalls on the
[L896] threshold.

[L981] What Counts as a Thread: Plot Versus Value
[L982] Two different things get called by plot letters, and only one of them is actually a plot. A
[L983] plot strand, my A, B, C, and sometimes D, is a line of action: its own events, its own track,
[L984] something actually happening. The feud is a line of action. Francine's secret game is a
[L985] line of action. An arc or a value, enemies becoming friends, respect, loneliness turning to
[L986] connection, is not a line of action. It is what a strand means, the cargo it carries. It rides
[L987] on a plot strand; it is not a strand of its own. That is the two-axes idea stated once and
[L988] cleanly: the values ride the plot lines, so I never mistake a value for a thread. Most guides
[L989] blur this, which is how a writer ends up thinking she has four plots when she has two
[L990] plots carrying four meanings.

[L993] feud is the A story's external action; the friendship is the arc that action produces, the
[L994] same thread named by where it starts and where it lands. So the book runs mainly on
[L995] two lines of action. A is the feud, Kevin against Anthony, and it carries two values as its
[L996] cargo, respect on the surface and the men moving from isolation to friendship
[L997] underneath. B is Francine, her own separate line of action, the hidden game, plus her
[L998] own arc from invisible to alive, and it is a true second thread because she runs her own
[L999] track until it collides with the men's at the reveal. The men's friendship was never a C. It

[L1009] the A feud and the B game together while deepening the men's arc.

[L1011] How the threads wrap. How they end matters as much as how they weave. In a novel or
[L1012] a film, the threads converge at the climax and resolve together, which is exactly what

[L1017] viewer into next week, and the season finale then converges the long threads the way a
[L1018] film's climax does. Same principle, different timing: always know which of your threads
[L1019] resolve now and which you are deliberately holding open.

[L1376] From Beats to Scenes: The Board and the Scene Engine
[L1377] The fifteen beats are the skeleton. Two more tools turn them into an actual draft: Snyder's
[L1378] board, which expands the beats into about forty scene cards, and the scene-and-sequel loop,
[L1379] which is how each individual scene is built and chained to the next. Both are on my wall;
[L1380] here is how to use them on this book.

[L1417] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 38 / 57>
[L1418] What it is. Every individual scene is one of two kinds, and they alternate to create the
[L1419] pulse of a novel. This is Dwight Swain's model, which underlies Ingermanson's Proactive
[L1420] and Reactive scenes, and my wall poster lays out the full emotional circle.

[L1422]   • A Scene (Proactive): Goal, Conflict, Disaster. The point-of-view character wants
[L1423]      something (Goal). Something blocks it (Conflict). And instead of simply succeeding,
[L1424]      they hit a Disaster that pushes them sideways rather than letting them advance in a
[L1425]      straight line to their story goal. The disaster is McKee's gap cracking open,
[L1426]      expectation versus result.




[L1431]   • A Sequel (Reactive): Reaction, Dilemma, Decision, New Goal. The disaster only
[L1432]      matters through the character's response. They React (emotionally, first). They face
[L1433]      a Dilemma (the disaster created a new set of problems with no good options). They
[L1434]      make a Decision about what to do next. And that decision becomes the New Goal
[L1435]      that launches the next Scene, so the whole thing comes full circle and pulls the
[L1436]      reader forward.
[L1437] Why they must alternate. The alternation is not decoration, it is the book breathing. A
[L1438] Scene is the inhale, the character pushing outward toward a goal and hitting a disaster. A
[L1439] Sequel is the exhale, the character absorbing the blow, weighing bad options, and
[L1440] choosing. Run nothing but Scenes and the reader suffocates, blow after blow with no
[L1441] room to feel any of them. Run nothing but Sequels and the story sits in a chair and
[L1442] thinks, going nowhere. The Sequel is also where most of the meaning and the emotion
[L1443] live, because a disaster the character never reacts to did not really happen to anyone,
[L1444] and a decision made without a felt dilemma costs nothing. So the rhythm itself does the
[L1445] work: push, absorb, choose, push again, and the choice at the end of each Sequel is the
[L1446] hook that drags the reader into the next Scene.

[L1448]    One way I could play it, not a decision yet: A Proactive scene for Kevin: Goal, he
[L1449]    wants to prove Anthony planted the fish guts. Conflict, he can find no evidence and
[L1450]    looks unhinged searching for it. Disaster, his snooping gets him caught by a
[L1451]    neighbor and makes him look like the guilty one, pushing him sideways into deeper
[L1452]    suspicion. Then a Sequel: Reaction, humiliation and rage; Dilemma, retaliate and
[L1453]    look crazier, or retreat and look weak; Decision, escalate but smarter, which
[L1454]    becomes the Goal of his next scene. The loop turns.

[L1590] Part Five: Narrative Devices and Tone
[L1591] How the book is told. These are structural decisions as much as style, and several of them
[L1592] carry my misdirection.

[L1594] Point of View: The Delivery System for the Secret
[L1595] What it is, and what it controls. Point of view is not a style choice about pronouns. It is
[L1596] the control valve on information, the decision about whose eyes the reader borrows and
[L1597] therefore what the reader is allowed to know, and when. Everything the reader learns,
[L1598] they learn through someone, so choosing the someone is choosing the blind spots. In an
[L1599] ordinary story that is a craft decision. In a story built on a hidden truth, like this one, it is
[L1600] the single most powerful structural choice I make, because the secret can only be kept by
[L1601] never handing myself the eyes that would see it.

[L1603] Why it works, and the principle that protects the secret. Here is the principle, close to
[L1604] a law for a misdirection story: keep the secret-keeper outside the point of view until I am
[L1605] ready to reveal them. If Francine ever narrates before the reveal, even for a paragraph, I
[L1606] am inside her head, and I cannot sit inside a schemer's head without either showing her
[L1607] scheming, which kills the surprise, or hiding her thoughts while pretending to share
[L1608] them, which is a cheat the reader can smell. So I never give myself that access. Kevin and
[L1609] Anthony carry the eyes; Francine is only ever seen from the outside, a sweet old lady
[L1610] with a garden, which traps the reader in the exact blind spot the men are in. The reveal
[L1611] then lands like a thunderclap, and it lands fair, because the reader can look back and see
[L1612] I never lied, I just never gave them Francine. And there is a gift inside the withholding:
[L1613] the first time I finally drop into her point of view, at or just after the reveal, all the
[L1614] hidden cunning and all the ache about the garden flood in at once, so the absence itself
[L1615] becomes the payoff.

[L1617] How it fails. Two failures, and both are quiet. The first is head-hopping, drifting from
[L1618] Kevin's head into Anthony's inside a single scene, because the moment the reader cannot
[L1619] trust whose knowledge they are getting, the misdirection stops being fair and starts
[L1620] feeling like a trick. The discipline is one point of view per scene or chapter, held without
[L1621] exception. The second is the slow leak, giving the reader a stray line of Francine's
[L1622] interior, a knowing thought, a private smile rendered from the inside, long before the
[L1623] reveal. One such slip and the reader half-knows, and the thunderclap becomes a mere
[L1624] confirmation. Landing: three-quarters of the book spent certain it is a two-man war, and
[L1625] then the floor drops out. Failing: a reader who by the midpoint has already thought, it is
[L1626] probably the old lady, because a few lines let her leak.

[L1631] Alternating Point of View Is Not Head-Hopping
[L1632] Multiple point of view, done right. This is the distinction that most confuses writers,
[L1633] and it is worth getting exactly right, because the book uses multiple point of view on
[L1634] purpose and the rule above could sound like it forbids that. It does not. Multiple point of
[L1635] view, done right, means one head per scene or per chapter. Kevin narrates this chapter
[L1636] from start to finish, and for the length of it the reader gets only what Kevin knows, sees,
[L1637] and suspects. Then, at a clean scene break or a chapter break, the camera is handed to
[L1638] Anthony, and the next stretch belongs entirely to him, only what he knows. The reader
[L1639] always knows whose eyes they are borrowing, because the switch happens at a seam
[L1640] they can see. That is not a flaw to avoid; it is one of the strongest engines this book has.

[L1642] Why two narrators are a gift. Two feuding narrators let the reader hold more than
[L1643] either man does. In Kevin's chapters the reader learns things Anthony cannot see, and in
[L1644] Anthony's chapters the reverse, so the reader sits above the feud watching each man
[L1645] confidently misread the other, which is comedy the structure generates for free. It also
[L1646] deepens the dramatic irony already running through the book: the reader, riding both
[L1647] men, stays a step ahead of each one, which is the very posture that makes the Francine
[L1648] reveal land, because the reader has spent the whole book feeling smart and is about to
[L1649] learn they were a step behind her the entire time.

[L1651] What head-hopping actually is. Head-hopping is a different thing entirely, and this is
[L1652] the line I do not cross. Head-hopping is switching heads inside a single continuous scene,
[L1653] with no break. The reader is in Kevin's thoughts, and then in the same scene, the same
[L1654] unbroken moment, they are suddenly inside Anthony's thoughts, then back again. The
[L1655] damage is that the reader loses track of whose knowledge they are holding, and trust
[L1656] goes out with it. In a misdirection book the damage is worse, because the instant the
[L1657] reader is allowed into everyone's head at once, I have quietly handed them access to the
[L1658] very truth I am trying to withhold. Landing: a chapter that is all Kevin, then a chapter
[L1659] that is all Anthony, and the reader never once wonders whose head they are in. Failing: a

why.

[L1692] The “In Which” Chapter Titles
[L1693] What it is. An old comic-novel tradition (Fielding, Dickens, Gaiman) of titling chapters
[L1694] “In which the whole world comes to an end.” The grand language takes a small event
[L1695] completely seriously, and the gap is the joke. It also carries dramatic irony: the title can
[L1696] mean one thing to Kevin and another to the reader who suspects Francine.

[L1698] Why it works. Start with where the joke actually lives, because it is not where most
[L1699] writers look for it. Voice does not only live in sentences; it can live in the architecture of

[L1704] the book, and a chapter title is the first and cheapest place to let it. The “In Which”
[L1705] formula is the narrator stepping forward, before a single line of the chapter, to announce
[L1706] what is coming in a voice with an attitude. And the way it turns funny is the same
[L1707] machine you have been drilling all along, run in miniature: understatement, irony, and
[L1708] misdirection. The grand phrasing takes a small event completely seriously, with a
[L1709] straight face, and the reader laughs at the gap between the operatic language and the
[L1710] tiny real thing. “In Which the Whole World Comes to an End,” sitting over a chapter
[L1711] where a man's pie gets snubbed at a block party, is the pattern-of-proportion joke you
[L1712] already know, now printed in the table of contents.

[L1714] The second job, dramatic irony. There is a second thing the title can do that makes it
[L1715] more than a laugh, and it is the reason this device is almost unfair for your book in
[L1716] particular. A good “In Which” title can mean one thing to the character and another to
[L1717] the reader, and that doubleness is dramatic irony working right in the heading. “In
[L1718] Which the Raccoons Choose a Side” reads to Kevin and Anthony as chaos out of nowhere.
[L1719] To a reader who already suspects Francine, it reads as her move landing, the varmints

[L1722] miniature, the surface meaning and the hidden one sitting in a single line.

[L1731] Which Kevin's Car Won't Start” fails, because it is a flat summary, true and dead, with no

### CHATGPT | 2026-10-14 10:14 ET | text

Oh, now we're getting somewhere! Because what you've just described takes this from a story-mapping tool to something much more interesting: **a visual novel architecture and development system.**

And no, I don't think it's too much for one program to do.

I do think it would be too much for one *screen* to display, and that's an important distinction.

The challenge isn't whether we can capture all these elements. We can. The challenge is designing a system that understands how they relate to one another without becoming so complicated that using it feels like a second job.

I've been thinking about this in relation to *I Declare War*, and there are several additions I'd recommend.

## 1. We need a hierarchy of dramatic units

You're remembering an important concept from Robert McKee's *Story*.

McKee describes a progression of dramatic units:

**Beat → Scene → Sequence → Act → Story**

Each level represents an increasingly significant change in a character's situation or story value.

| Level | Purpose | What we should track |
|---|---|---|
| **Beat** | The smallest meaningful exchange of action and reaction | What changes during the interaction |
| **Scene** | A unit of action that produces a meaningful value change | Goal, conflict, outcome, value before and after |
| **Sequence** | A collection of scenes that produces a larger turning point | Sequence goal, escalation, cumulative value change |
| **Act** | A major movement of the story culminating in a significant reversal | Act objective, major conflict, turning point, value shift |
| **Story** | The complete dramatic journey | Controlling idea, overall transformation, final value |

And this is where your idea becomes especially valuable.

### Every level should have its own objective and outcome.

Let's use the fish-guts sequence from *I Declare War*.

Suppose Anthony discovers a terrible smell in his yard.

**Scene 1: The mysterious smell**

Anthony's goal: Determine where the smell is coming from.

Conflict: He cannot find the source.

Initial value: Control (+)

Final value: Uncertainty (-)

**Scene 2: The animals arrive**

Anthony's goal: Get the animals out of his yard.

Conflict: His attempts make the situation increasingly ridiculous.

Initial value: Control (+)

Final value: Humiliation (-)

**Scene 3: Anthony confronts Kevin**

Anthony's goal: Force Kevin to confess.

Conflict: Kevin denies involvement and retaliates against the accusation.

Initial value: Superiority (+)

Final value: Frustration (-)

These are hypothetical scene divisions, not established decisions from your bible.

Now consider the sequence as a whole.

**Sequence objective:** Anthony attempts to regain control of his home and dignity.

**Sequence value:** Security → Humiliation

**Sequence outcome:** Anthony wrongly concludes that Kevin is responsible, escalating the war.

The sequence creates a new problem that drives the next sequence.

And the key is that the **sequence has its own dramatic arc**, beyond the individual scenes composing it.

That is exactly what we should capture.

### One refinement I'd make

Not every scene must begin positive and end negative. A scene can move from negative to positive, and the value can change in degree rather than simply flipping signs.

McKee's value shifts can be nuanced:

- Positive to negative
- Negative to positive
- Positive to more positive
- Negative to more negative
- Apparently positive to secretly negative

That last one is especially useful for *I Declare War*, because Francine can create situations that appear to benefit one of the men while actually advancing her own objective.

I'd want the system to record both **the apparent value shift and the actual value shift** when those differ.

That's a powerful feature for mysteries, thrillers, and stories built around dramatic irony.

## 2. Cause and effect should be a first-class feature

This is something I feel strongly about.

Most writing software lets authors arrange scenes.

But arranging scenes chronologically isn't the same as understanding their causal relationships.

Consider these two constructions:

**Chronological:**
Scene 1 happens. Then Scene 2 happens. Then Scene 3 happens.

**Causal:**
Because Scene 1 happens, the character makes a decision that triggers Scene 2. The outcome of Scene 2 makes Scene 3 unavoidable.

The second is storytelling.

I would want our system to track:

**Cause → Action → Consequence → Reaction → Decision → Next Action**

This corresponds beautifully with the Scene and Sequel framework already included in your story bible.

For each scene, the system could ask:

- What caused this scene?
- What does the viewpoint character want?
- What opposes that goal?
- What actually happens?
- What story value changes?
- What new problem or opportunity emerges?
- What decision follows?
- Which scene does that decision cause?

And here's an important addition.

**A scene should be able to cause multiple subsequent scenes.**

For example, Francine's fish-guts prank could simultaneously trigger Anthony's animal crisis, Kevin's paranoia, and a neighborhood reaction.

That's branching causality.

An eventual visual map could show those branches and where they converge.

## 3. We need two different timelines

You raised the question of whether the novel happens over a week, a month, a season, or a year.

That's important enough that I'd create two separate but synchronized timelines.

### Timeline One: Narrative Position

This shows where events occur in the manuscript.

For example:

- Scene 12
- Act Two
- Fun and Games
- Approximately 30% through the manuscript
- Around page 75 of a 250-page novel
- Around page 90 of a 300-page novel

### Timeline Two: Storyworld Time

This tracks when events occur inside the fictional world.

For example:

- Tuesday, June 16
- 7:30 a.m.
- Anthony's backyard
- Approximately 36 hours after the previous major incident
- Third day of the neighborhood feud

Those are illustrative details, not decisions about your novel.

Why separate the two?

Because **narrative order and chronological order aren't necessarily the same.**

An author may employ flashbacks, flash-forwards, overlapping points of view, or events revealed after they occur.

And for your novel, Francine's secret actions might happen before the scenes in which Kevin and Anthony experience their consequences.

This means we should track at least three things:

1. When an event actually happens.
2. When the reader encounters it.
3. When the characters learn about it.

That third dimension could become one of the program's most distinctive features.

## 4. Location and atmosphere deserve their own architecture

I wouldn't simply make a field called "Location."

I'd establish a **Storyworld Database**.

For *I Declare War*, that might begin with the neighborhood itself.

Then we'd define its physical spaces:

**The neighborhood**
- Street configuration
- House positions
- Sidewalks and driveways
- Common areas
- Neighbors' sightlines
- Where characters can observe one another

**Kevin's property**
- House
- Driveway
- Garage
- Front yard
- Backyard
- Interior rooms relevant to scenes

**Anthony's property**
- House
- Front yard
- Backyard
- Areas where the animal siege unfolds

**Francine's property**
- House
- Porch
- Garden
- Locations where she can observe or manipulate events
- Where she keeps her ledger

These aren't necessarily all established locations. They're the kinds of spaces we'd define as needed.

And each location should have relationships with the others.

For instance:

**Can Francine see Anthony's backyard from her porch?**

That sounds like a minor geographic question.

But it could determine whether an entire scene is physically plausible.

### Then we add atmosphere.

For every scene, we could optionally track:

| Dimension | Examples |
|---|---|
| Season | Spring, summer, autumn, winter |
| Time of day | Dawn, morning, afternoon, evening, night |
| Weather | Sunny, humid, rainy, stormy |
| Physical atmosphere | Quiet, crowded, chaotic, oppressive |
| Emotional atmosphere | Suspicious, playful, hostile, intimate |
| Sensory details | Smells, sounds, light, temperature |
| Environmental consequences | Mud after rain, heat affecting odors, darkness limiting visibility |

The fish-guts sequence illustrates why this matters.

A hot summer afternoon produces a very different experience from a cool autumn morning.

Weather isn't always background decoration.

Sometimes it participates in the plot.

## 5. We should track dramatic tension separately from scene values

Here's an addition I think would be tremendously useful.

**Story value and tension are not the same thing.**

A scene can move from humiliation to dignity while tension increases.

A scene can also move from danger to safety while tension decreases.

I'd track at least three different dimensions:

**Story value:** What meaningful condition changes?

**Tension:** How much uncertainty, danger, opposition, or anticipation exists?

**Emotional intensity:** How strongly does the moment affect the characters or reader?

For a comedy, I would add a fourth:

**Comic intensity.**

Imagine being able to view the entire novel with a visual rhythm showing:

Comedy rises.

Tension rises.

Comedy peaks.

Tension falls briefly.

The midpoint changes the stakes.

Tension rebuilds.

All Is Lost delivers the deepest reversal.

The Confession lets genuine vulnerability emerge.

The finale combines laughter, tension, and emotional payoff.

This would help you avoid a manuscript that feels emotionally flat even when plenty of things are happening.

And we shouldn't assume that maximum laughter must always coincide with maximum dramatic tension.

Sometimes the quietest scene carries the greatest emotional weight.

## 6. Track character knowledge, beliefs, and misconceptions

Your bible already contains a reader-knowledge timeline.

I would expand that concept.

For every important revelation, the system could distinguish:

| Dimension | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Actual truth | What really happened |
| Character knowledge | What each character knows |
| Character belief | What each character thinks happened |
| Reader knowledge | What the reader has been told |
| Reader suspicion | What the narrative encourages the reader to suspect |
| Revelation | When the truth becomes known |

This is particularly important because a character can possess information but interpret it incorrectly.

Kevin might know that Anthony wasn't home during an incident but still believe Anthony arranged it.

That's different from Kevin having no information at all.

And those differences are where some of your best comedy and misdirection could originate.

**I'd consider this feature essential for your novel, but optional for other genres.**

That's an important distinction for the eventual program.

Not every author needs every tool.

## 7. Track setups, payoffs, and narrative promises

Your story bible already has a plant-and-payoff tracker, but I'd expand it into a relationship system.

A setup might connect to multiple payoffs.

A payoff might depend on several earlier setups.

Consider Francine's ledger.

It serves several functions:

- Establishes her habit of keeping score.
- Expresses something about her personality.
- Documents the actual cause of events.
- Provides the means of revealing her involvement.
- Gives the men leverage during the finale.

That's one object doing several storytelling jobs.

The eventual system should allow the author to associate an object, action, line of dialogue, or recurring motif with multiple narrative functions.

And I would add a useful diagnostic:

**Unpaid Promises**

The system could flag significant setups that have no identified payoff.

Not every detail needs to pay off, of course.

But if an author deliberately plants something important, they should be able to see whether it eventually earns its place.

## 8. We need to track conflict at multiple levels

This is another concept that fits the McKee framework.

A story has conflict operating at different scales.

### Internal conflict

Kevin's paranoia and desire for respect.

### Interpersonal conflict

Kevin versus Anthony.

### External or environmental conflict

The increasingly chaotic neighborhood circumstances.

But I would add **conflicting character objectives within individual scenes**.

For example:

Kevin wants Anthony to admit wrongdoing.

Anthony wants Kevin to lose his composure.

Both might achieve what they want.

Or both might fail.

Or one might appear to win while actually making his situation worse.

Imagine clicking a scene and seeing a concise conflict diagram:

**Kevin's objective → Opposing objective → Turning action → Outcome**

Then seeing how that outcome contributes to the sequence objective.

That would make it much easier to diagnose scenes that feel entertaining but aren't advancing the story.

## 9. Track motifs and recurring story elements

This is something you haven't explicitly mentioned, but I think it belongs in the system.

A motif isn't necessarily a plot point.

It may be an image, object, behavior, phrase, or situation whose meaning develops throughout the novel.

For *I Declare War*, possible motifs include:

- The garden
- The car
- The ledger
- The act of watching neighbors
- The children's card game
- Being seen versus being overlooked

The garden is particularly interesting.

Early in the story, it's something the men barely acknowledge.

Later, the reader discovers it's the motivation behind everything.

At the end, it becomes the visible center of connection.

That's a meaningful transformation of a recurring story element.

I'd want the system to track **where motifs appear and how their meaning changes**.

This could be a particularly valuable tool for literary fiction, historical fiction, and complex multigenerational stories.

## 10. The program should distinguish planning from actual drafting

This may be one of the most important features we haven't discussed.

Right now, we're talking about planning a novel.

But once you start drafting, the plan and the manuscript may diverge.

And that's perfectly normal.

So I would create two related states:

**Planned Story**

What the author currently intends to happen.

**Written Story**

What actually exists in the manuscript.

For example:

| Element | Planned | Drafted |
|---|---|---|
| Catalyst | 10% | 13% |
| Midpoint | 50% | 54% |
| All Is Lost | 75% | Not drafted |
| Confession | Dark Night | Not drafted |

These are hypothetical values.

The system could show where the manuscript differs from the planned architecture without automatically treating those differences as mistakes.

That's critical.

**A writing tool should inform the author, not police the author.**

Sometimes the scene that emerges organically is better than the one originally planned.

The program should help the writer recognize and evaluate that change.

## 11. I would add a decision and revision history

You specifically said the system needs to be editable.

Absolutely.

But I would go further.

**It should remember how the story evolved.**

Suppose you initially place the block party pie scene at 35%.

Later, you decide it belongs closer to the midpoint.

You move it.

That change may affect the sequence containing it, the pacing of the surrounding scenes, and the placement of earlier setups.

Ideally, the program could show you which elements are connected to the moved scene.

Not necessarily force changes, but identify potential consequences.

And it should preserve the earlier version so you can reverse the decision if necessary.

For me, that suggests three core capabilities:

**Flexible editing:** Add, remove, rename, move, or revise any story element.

**Dependency awareness:** See what other elements may be affected by a change.

**Version history:** Recover previous structural decisions without losing your work.

I would also preserve your existing distinction between:

- Decided
- Working possibility
- Undecided

And perhaps add a fourth:

**Drafted and confirmed**

Because something you've actually written may become more authoritative than something you previously planned.

## 12. One additional feature: story diagnostics

Now this is where I see an eventual program becoming genuinely useful.

Rather than merely displaying the author's information, it could analyze the relationships among that information.

For example, it might identify:

**Causality gaps:** A scene happens without a clear cause.

**Dead-end scenes:** A scene has no meaningful consequence or connection to later developments.

**Missing value turns:** A scene doesn't produce a detectable story-value change.

**Sequence weaknesses:** Several scenes occur without collectively producing a meaningful reversal.

**Character disappearance:** An important character vanishes from the narrative for an unexpectedly long stretch.

**Unresolved setups:** A deliberate plant lacks an identified payoff.

**Timeline contradictions:** A character appears in two places at the same time.

**Knowledge inconsistencies:** A character acts on information they haven't yet acquired.

**Pacing concerns:** A major beat falls substantially outside the author's intended placement.

**Thematic disconnects:** Important scenes have no clear relationship to the novel's controlling idea.

But I'd have the system present these as **questions worth investigating**, not automatic declarations that something is wrong.

A missing value turn might be intentional.

A long character absence might be necessary.

A surprising structural choice might be precisely what makes a novel distinctive.

An intelligent tool needs to respect the author's creative judgment.

# 13. Now, about your concern that this might be too much for one program

I think the answer depends on how we architect it.

Trying to build a single enormous application in which every capability is tightly interconnected would be difficult to maintain.

But building **one program with a shared story database and specialized modules** is entirely reasonable.

Here's how I'd organize it.

| Module | Primary responsibility |
|---|---|
| Story Foundation | Logline, premise, genre, theme, controlling idea |
| Narrative Architecture | Acts, sequences, scenes, beats, turning points |
| Plot Engine | A/B/C stories, causal relationships, conflicts |
| Character Arcs | Wants, needs, lies, transformations |
| Storyworld | Locations, physical geography, chronology, atmosphere |
| Dramatic Values | Scene changes, sequence changes, act-level transformations |
| Knowledge & Revelation | Secrets, misconceptions, reader information |
| Narrative Threads | Setups, payoffs, motifs, recurring elements |
| Drafting & Revision | Planned versus written structure, progress, history |
| Story Diagnostics | Consistency checks, structural questions, potential weaknesses |
| Visualization Studio | Generate and customize the different story maps |

And the key architectural principle would be:

**Enter information once. Use it everywhere.**

For instance, if you define a scene within the Plot Engine, that same scene should automatically appear in the Narrative Architecture, Storyworld timeline, Character Arc view, and whichever posters include it.

You shouldn't need to enter the same information five times.

That's how we keep a sophisticated program from becoming exhausting.

# 14. There's something else I want to protect: the joy of writing

This is particularly important for you.

Your story bible begins with an acknowledgment that you can hold an enormous amount of information in your mind, but that this sometimes becomes overwhelming.

The bible was explicitly designed to help you move from knowing what to do to actually writing.

I don't want us to accidentally create a system so sophisticated that maintaining it becomes more compelling than finishing *I Declare War*.

That's a genuine risk.

Especially for someone who enjoys developing intricate creative systems.

So here's a principle I would build into the software from the beginning:

### Progressive complexity

An author should be able to begin with nothing more than:

**I have an idea about two neighbors who go to war.**

That's enough to create a basic story map.

As the author develops the story, they can add characters, sequences, scenes, values, locations, timelines, and relationships.

The map grows with the novel.

There should never be a requirement to complete an enormous questionnaire before using the program.

And I'd want a very simple way to capture an idea when it strikes.

Perhaps an author types:

*Francine should have a habit of writing things down in her garden journal.*

The program could propose linking that idea to her character, the setup, the ledger reveal, and the finale.

The author approves the relevant relationships.

Then the maps update.

That's a much more natural creative workflow than making the author manually complete several database forms.

# 15. Here's the feature I'd personally be most excited about

**The ability to move between different levels of narrative detail without losing your place.**

Imagine this:

You're looking at the entire novel on your 48 × 36-inch poster.

You select Act Two.

Now you're looking at the sequences within Act Two.

You select the animal-siege sequence.

Now you're looking at its scenes, arranged chronologically.

You select Anthony's confrontation with Kevin.

Now you're looking at:

- The viewpoint character
- The scene objective
- The opposition
- The inciting action
- The turning point
- The initial and final story values
- The emotional change
- The time and location
- The preceding cause
- The resulting consequence
- The next scene

That's **narrative zoom**.

And I think it's the conceptual heart of the entire program.

You can zoom out to see the forest.

Zoom in to examine a tree.

And zoom out again without losing the relationship between them.

For a writer managing a complex novel, that would be enormously useful.

It also gives us a solution to the poster problem.

Your three printable maps would represent different views of the same underlying architecture, while the eventual application would allow you to explore that architecture interactively.

# 16. My recommendation: build the foundation with future expansion in mind

I wouldn't attempt to develop all these features simultaneously.

I'd approach this in three stages.

**Stage One: Build the mapping architecture using *I Declare War*.**

Define the information model, scene hierarchy, relationships, timelines, story values, and visual conventions.

Produce the three printable maps.

This lets us discover what actually works when used for a real novel.

**Stage Two: Make the maps editable and interconnected.**

Introduce the ability to modify individual elements and regenerate the posters without manually rebuilding everything.

At this point, we'd have a functional story-mapping tool.

**Stage Three: Generalize it for other authors.**

Add customizable structures, alternative plotting frameworks, genre-specific modules, drafting integration, diagnostics, and more sophisticated visualization.

Importantly, the eventual program should not force every novel into Save the Cat or McKee.

Those are frameworks the author can choose to use, not universal rules the software should impose.

## And one final thought

I would distinguish three different kinds of relationships throughout the system:

**Structural relationships:** This scene belongs to this sequence, which belongs to this act.

**Causal relationships:** This event causes that consequence, which triggers another event.

**Thematic relationships:** This scene expresses or transforms a particular story value, character belief, or thematic idea.

Those three relationship types are fundamentally different.

And if we model them properly, we can generate a remarkable variety of visualizations from the same underlying information.

That's what makes your idea technically feasible.

We don't need to create a different database for each poster.

We need **one interconnected representation of the novel that can be viewed from different perspectives.**

### What I would add to our immediate planning

Before we create the first poster, I'd like us to establish one additional element:

**A story-map legend and visual language.**

For example, a visual convention that distinguishes:

- Plot strands
- Character arcs
- Story values
- Sequence boundaries
- Major turning points
- Causal relationships
- Thematic relationships
- Setups and payoffs
- Confirmed versus unresolved material

That consistent visual language would carry across all three poster designs and, eventually, the interactive application.

It would mean learning to read the maps once, rather than having to interpret a different system every time.

**And my answer to your larger question is this: No, you're not asking too much of one program. You're describing a coherent system with several interconnected capabilities.**

The challenge is ensuring that the program remains a tool for writing novels rather than becoming another enormous creative project that prevents the novel from getting written.

So my proposed guiding principle is:

**The system should understand the complexity of the story so the author doesn't have to carry all that complexity in her head.**

That's what I think we're really building.

**Adaptability. Yes! And I think you've just identified one of the most important architectural requirements for the entire program.**

Because we're developing our first three posters around *I Declare War*, a comedy, there's a danger of unconsciously designing a comedy-writing system and then trying to retrofit it for other genres.

I don't want us to make that mistake.

We should design a **genre-independent storytelling engine with genre-aware intelligence.**

Those are two different things.

## 1. The fundamental story architecture should be genre-independent

The foundational elements we've discussed apply to many forms of storytelling:

- Characters have objectives, motivations, and conflicts.
- Events have causes and consequences.
- Scenes produce changes in circumstances or story values.
- Scenes form sequences, sequences form acts, and acts form the complete narrative.
- Stories develop themes, relationships, and dramatic tension.
- Information is revealed or withheld.
- Authors establish expectations and deliver payoffs.

These principles can help organize a comedy, mystery, thriller, horror novel, romance, historical novel, fantasy, or literary novel.

However, **the way those elements function can differ dramatically between genres.**

And that's where the program's intelligence needs to become more sophisticated.

## 2. Genre should influence the analysis, not dictate the story

Consider how our system might approach different genres.

| Genre | Important narrative considerations |
|---|---|
| **Comedy** | Character-driven humor, comic escalation, incongruity, reversals, timing, emotional payoff |
| **Mystery** | Clues, suspects, investigative logic, red herrings, fair revelations, information control |
| **Thriller** | Threat escalation, urgency, suspense, reversals, stakes, vulnerability |
| **Horror** | Fear, uncertainty, atmosphere, dread, vulnerability, escalating threats |
| **Romance** | Relationship development, emotional intimacy, internal barriers, romantic conflict, satisfying resolution |
| **Fantasy** | Worldbuilding, magic systems, internal rules, character objectives, consequences |
| **Science Fiction** | Speculative premises, technological or scientific consistency, societal implications, causality |
| **Historical Fiction** | Historical context, chronology, setting authenticity, character agency |
| **Literary Fiction** | Character complexity, thematic development, narrative form, psychological transformation |

These are considerations, not mandatory checklists.

For example, a horror novel doesn't necessarily need escalating physical violence to become frightening. Psychological dread and uncertainty may be far more important.

Similarly, a mystery doesn't necessarily need a conventional detective or a murder.

The program should understand genre conventions without confusing them with requirements.

### Genre blending is equally important.

*I Declare War* is a comedy, but its hidden manipulation and eventual revelation also use techniques associated with mysteries.

The system should recognize that.

An author might describe a novel as:

**Primary genre:** Comedy  
**Secondary influences:** Mystery, satire  
**Narrative characteristics:** Misdirection, dramatic irony, hidden antagonist

That combination should inform the diagnostic tools and resource suggestions.

A romantic thriller should receive guidance appropriate to both its romantic and suspense elements.

And an author should be free to change those classifications whenever the story evolves.

## 3. Adaptability must extend beyond genre

Here's where I would expand your principle.

**Adaptability should operate across five dimensions.**

### A. Genre adaptability

The system understands genre-specific conventions, expectations, and narrative techniques.

### B. Structural adaptability

Authors can choose their preferred storytelling frameworks or work without one.

We shouldn't force everyone into Save the Cat's 15 beats.

Someone might use three-act structure, four-act structure, the Hero's Journey, the Snowflake Method, or a completely custom architecture.

We should also avoid treating the scene, sequence, act, and story hierarchy as universally mandatory.

It's a useful analytical model, not the only legitimate way to construct fiction.

### C. Process adaptability

Some authors meticulously outline before drafting.

Others discover the story while writing.

Many fall somewhere between those approaches.

The program should support all three.

An author shouldn't have to create a complete plot map before writing the first chapter.

### D. Complexity adaptability

A relatively straightforward contemporary romance might require only a few story threads.

An epic fantasy could involve multiple protagonists, timelines, locations, and interconnected conflicts.

The underlying system should handle both without making the simpler story unnecessarily complicated.

### E. Author adaptability

This may be the most important dimension.

Different authors think differently.

Some understand their stories chronologically.

Others visualize relationships.

Some think primarily in character arcs, while others think in dramatic sequences or thematic patterns.

That's precisely why your three-poster idea is so valuable.

**The story remains the same. The representation adapts to the author's mind.**

And I would carry that principle into the eventual application.

## 4. Let's establish a firm rule for resource recommendations

I agree with your decision completely.

**The program will not recommend specific chapters or page numbers in books.**

Instead, it will recommend:

- A relevant book, article, website, or other reputable educational resource.
- The author or creator.
- The storytelling concept that makes the resource relevant.
- A concise explanation of why the author might find it useful.

For example:

**Identified concern:** The motivation connecting two scenes may be insufficient.

**Relevant craft concept:** Scene causality and the relationship between character goals, conflict, and consequences.

**Suggested resource:** Robert McKee's *Story*.

**Why:** McKee's approach to dramatic structure and the gap between expectation and result may offer useful ways to examine the connection.

No chapter references.

No page numbers.

No pretending that the author needs to study a particular passage to fix the problem.

For websites and articles, we can provide direct links when available and verified.

I'd also want the program to distinguish between **established references, author-supplied resources, and newly discovered recommendations**.

That would make the system's advice more transparent.

## 5. I want to introduce one additional concept: genre expectations versus author intentions

Suppose someone writes a mystery in which the culprit's identity is revealed halfway through the novel.

A conventional mystery-analysis tool might flag that as a structural weakness.

But what if the author deliberately reveals the culprit because the real narrative question is whether anyone can prove the crime?

Now the program needs to understand that the author is writing a different kind of mystery.

It should evaluate the author's intended effect rather than insist on a standard structure.

That means the eventual system should ask an important question:

**What experience is the author trying to create for the reader?**

Suspense?

Dread?

Laughter?

Wonder?

Heartbreak?

Romantic anticipation?

Intellectual curiosity?

A sense of discovery?

Several simultaneously?

The answers should inform how the program examines the manuscript.

For *I Declare War*, we're aiming for laughter, escalating absurdity, misdirection, and an ultimately meaningful emotional payoff.

But another author may intentionally want discomfort, ambiguity, or an unresolved ending.

Neither approach is inherently wrong.

The software's job is to help determine whether the story's construction supports its intended effect.

## 6. Adaptability also means the program itself should be extensible

We can't anticipate every genre, subgenre, storytelling method, or creative workflow.

Nor should we try.

I would design the eventual program with a common storytelling foundation and optional specialized capabilities.

For example:

**Core engine:** Narrative structure, scenes, sequences, character goals, value changes, causality, chronology, relationships, and visualization.

**Genre-aware capabilities:** Mystery clue tracking, romance relationship development, horror threat progression, fantasy world rules, and so forth.

**Author-defined capabilities:** Custom labels, story values, plot structures, relationship types, and analytical priorities.

That final category matters.

Authors should be able to create something we haven't anticipated.

We shouldn't require a software update every time someone invents a different way to structure a novel.

## 7. And here's one principle I'd add to our growing foundation

**The program should learn the author's creative intentions without attempting to replace them.**

Not merely remember their preferred genre.

It should understand their stated objectives, chosen framework, deliberate departures from convention, and previous decisions.

For example, if an author has explicitly decided to structure their novel around an unconventional midpoint, the program should take that intention into account when conducting later analyses.

This doesn't mean it can never question the decision.

It means any concern should be evaluated in the context of what the author is actually trying to accomplish.

That distinction is essential.

## Where we stand now

I think we have established six governing principles worth preserving in the eventual product specification.

| Principle | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Author sovereignty** | The author retains complete creative and editorial control. |
| **Adaptability** | The system accommodates different genres, structures, processes, complexity levels, and ways of thinking. |
| **Narrative integrity** | The system examines causality, dramatic values, structural relationships, and consistency. |
| **Transparency** | The system distinguishes structural facts from subjective interpretations and acknowledges uncertainty. |
| **Contextual guidance** | The system identifies relevant craft concepts and recommends resources without dictating solutions or citing book chapters and pages. |
| **Progressive complexity** | Authors can begin simply and expand their story architecture as needed. |

I would add a seventh:

**Creative momentum:** The system should help authors move toward completing their novels, not become another elaborate task that competes with writing.

And I think that's especially important as we return to our original objective.

### The next milestone remains the three *I Declare War* posters.

We now have a much clearer understanding of what they need to accomplish.

The chronological map will emphasize dramatic progression.

The relationship map will emphasize causality, thematic connections, and narrative dependencies.

The hybrid will integrate both perspectives into a comprehensive visual architecture.

All three will draw from the same underlying story information.

And although *I Declare War* is our first example, we'll design the information model so that it doesn't assume every story involves comedy, misdirection, or even a conventional three-act structure.

**One story. Multiple ways to understand it. Adaptable to the author, not the other way around.**

That, to me, is the foundation of the program we're envisioning.
